questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The interview as an interaction rather than a channel
questions.learningObjective: identify what a conception of interviewing as transmission leaves out
questions.stem: A member says an interview is just a way of putting questions to people and getting back what they know. What does that account of interviewing leave out?

options.text: That some things cannot be asked in an interview at all and have to be put in writing instead
options.misconception: moves to a different instrument without saying what the interview as used is doing to the answer

options.text: That the interviewer's conduct is itself part of what gets recorded, so the instrument is the person asking
That people hold knowledge they have never been asked about, and questions exist to draw it out
options.misconception: names a true fact about knowledge without identifying what is added by the act of asking

options.text: That people give different answers on different days, which is why any interview needs repeating
options.misconception: raises a genuine methodological point while leaving the instrument itself untouched

questions.explanation: The account treats the interview as a pipe, and the pipe has no bends in it. In practice the record is a product of the encounter: what was asked, in what order, with what follow-ups offered, in what tone, and who else was in the room all become part of the evidence, because those are things that change what a person says. A member who is offered a follow-up on the thing they mentioned in passing and a member who is not will produce different notes from the same conversation. The other three options are all true and none of them is the omission, and the last is a further step away from the question, which is about what this instrument does rather than about when to reach for a different one.
questions.hint: Ask what the transcript would look like if a different person had asked the same questions.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A question with two parts that the first part settles
questions.learningObjective: identify the part of a compound question that its second part inherits
questions.stem: An interviewer asks: how easy was it to get an appointment, and how satisfied were you with how it went? What will the second part of that question produce?

options.text: A second measure of the same thing, since ease and satisfaction are two names for one judgement
options.misconception: merges two distinct judgements, which is the confusion the compound question produces

options.text: An answer taken from the first part, since the two are joined and a respondent gives one verdict on both
An answer about satisfaction, since the word is a plain one and nobody is misled by it
options.misconception: assumes the wording settles the answer, where the binding is what does the work

options.text: A test of willingness to complain, since a bad first answer licenses a bad second one
options.misconception: supposes a deliberate design the question does not need in order to do its damage

questions.explanation: Asking a question about ease and then asking about satisfaction in the same breath produces one answer, because the respondent is answering the question as heard, and the first half is the part they can form a view on quickly. A person who found the appointment easy will tend to say they were satisfied, and a person who did not will tend to say they were not, and neither reply tells the group what the second question was for. The way to see the problem is to ask the two questions separately and on different occasions: the satisfaction answers move, and the movement is the finding. The fourth option reads the compound question as an instrument for something it does not need to be, and the first option mistakes the confusion for a fact about the constructs.
questions.hint: Ask the two halves separately, on different occasions, and see whether the second answer moves.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A question that carries the answer it wants
questions.learningObjective: recognise how a tagged question and its follow-up convert one claim into two answers

stimulus.kind: interview schedule written for this question
stimulus.body: Interview schedule written for this exercise. 'Q7. You would agree the new booking system cut the time you spend on the phone, would you not? Q8. How much time would you say that saved you: a few minutes, or a lot? The researcher's notes record that 9 of the 11 respondents said yes to Q7, and that the answers to Q8 were 8 few minutes, 1 a lot, 2 did not answer.'

questions.stem: What does the schedule do to the two sets of answers it collects?

options.text: It offers a closed pair of answers, so the respondent is choosing between two rather than estimating
options.misconception: identifies a real weakness of Q8 while ignoring the claim Q7 has already put into the record

options.text: It lets a respondent decline, since the schedule marks a place for the answer and two did not use it
options.misconception: reads the non-answers as evidence of free choice, when the question invited agreement throughout

options.text: It puts a claim in the question and then asks for a quantity, so both answers begin in the claim
It asks the same matter twice, so the second question is a check on the consistency of the first
options.misconception: reads a leading question plus a follow-up as a consistency check, which reverses what the pair does

questions.explanation: Q7 contains a claim and asks for assent to it, and assent is the path of least resistance, so nine yeses are close to what the wording alone would produce. Q8 then converts that assent into a magnitude, and a respondent who has just agreed that time was saved will rarely say it was not, which is why few minutes collects eight of the eleven. Neither number is a measurement of the booking system; both are measurements of the schedule. The first option names a genuine weakness and stops in the wrong place, since a closed pair of answers is a real limitation even with a neutrally worded Q7, and here the damage is already done one question earlier. The repair is to ask for the time first, unprompted and open, and only then ask whether the respondent attributes it to the system.
questions.hint: Ask what the respondent would have said if the first question had not proposed a conclusion.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Telling the participant what the study suspects
questions.learningObjective: assess what a leading introduction does to the answers that follow it

stimulus.kind: interview note written for this question
stimulus.body: Interview note written for this exercise. 'Before each interview the researcher said: we have found that people who book online come out of the appointment less anxious than people who telephone, and I would like to hear how you got on. The notes record that most respondents then described the online route as less stressful, and the write-up reports a difference of four to one in the proportion describing the online route as less stressful. The note also records that the introduction was shortened after the fourth interview because two respondents said the question already told them the answer.'

questions.stem: What does the record establish about the four to one difference?

options.text: That the introduction supplied the comparison, so the figure bears on the wording as much as on the routes
That the figure is sound, since reading a finding out is a way of checking whether people agree
options.misconception: treats agreement under instruction as corroboration, which is the mechanism that produced it

options.text: That the researcher wanted one route to look better, and so the figure reports the researcher's aim
options.misconception: reaches for the fallacy of origin, which needs evidence about the aim and not only about the wording

options.text: That a four to one difference is too large to have been produced by an introduction at all
options.misconception: asserts a bound on what a leading introduction can do, which nobody has established here

questions.explanation: The introduction told every respondent which two things to compare and which of them came out better, and the respondents then did the natural thing and agreed. The four to one therefore measures two routes and a wording, and the group cannot separate them. The note's own last sentence is the strongest evidence available: two respondents volunteered that the question had told them the answer, which is a report of the effect from inside the interview rather than an inference about it. Shortening the introduction afterwards does not repair the earlier interviews. The third option is the tempting one and it is wrong on this evidence, because nothing shows what the researcher wanted the result to be; the fourth sets a limit nobody has measured, and the honest verdict is that the figure's size is uninformative rather than implausible.
questions.hint: Ask what the respondent was told before being asked, and what agreement with it would mean.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Counting people who live together as separate observations
questions.learningObjective: identify the dependence hidden in a count of households
questions.stem: A group surveys 20 households and treats the 20 replies as 20 independent observations. Fifteen respondents described a shared household routine. What is the difficulty with the count?

options.text: Twenty is too few a number for any claim, so a survey of this size settles nothing at all
options.misconception: rules out the whole design on grounds of size, where the problem is what the size counts

options.text: The routine is private rather than shared, so a household reply cannot stand for a household's members
options.misconception: denies that routines are shared, which is precisely the pattern the group reported finding

options.text: Only one adult was asked per household, so nothing in the figure concerns the households at all
options.misconception: treats a sampling choice as though it deleted the object the group was asking about

options.text: Two adults in one household can report the same routine, so the 20 replies are not 20 separate looks

questions.explanation: A count of replies is a count of answers, and a count of independent observations is a different thing. Where the people answering share the routine under discussion, they are likely to give the same account, so the 15 agreements among 20 replies contain less independent information than 15 agreements among 20 strangers. A group can check how much the choice matters by asking how many households contained two of the respondents and whether the two agreed, and it should report the number of households rather than the number of replies. The first option is the over-correction that would empty small surveys of any content, and the third option treats a limitation as though it removed the object of study, when what a household does is exactly what the group wanted to know.
questions.hint: Ask how many of the 20 replies came from households with two adults in them.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The researcher's own stake showing in the answers
questions.learningObjective: state what an interview conducted by an interested party is evidence of
questions.stem: A researcher interviews members about a scheme the researcher helped design. Every reply praises the scheme and no reply names a cost. What is the strongest thing the group can say about the notes?

options.text: That praise is what a designer is equipped to hear, so the replies show what the researcher wanted
options.misconception: reports the bias without saying what the record is nonetheless good evidence of

options.text: That they record what was said in that room, and the room was one the researcher had arranged
That the members were insincere, since people do not criticise a scheme to the person who built it
options.misconception: asserts a state of mind the notes cannot show, and needs to assume the absence of criticism was felt

options.text: That the researcher's involvement voids the enquiry and no reply in it may be used at all
options.misconception: discards the usable part of the record along with the part that is only what it is

questions.explanation: The notes are good evidence of what was said in the room the researcher set up, and weak evidence of what members think, and both halves of that sentence are worth having. The uniform praise is not a finding about the scheme; it is a finding about a conversation in which every available answer supported the person who had built it. Practical repairs exist and are cheap: have someone else ask, ask in writing so nobody has to answer the designer, ask about a specific recent occasion rather than about the scheme, and ask what the scheme costs a member, which is a question with an answerable shape. The third option claims more than anyone knows, since members may simply have found nothing to criticise that they were asked about, and the fourth throws away the part of the record that does support statements about what people said.
questions.hint: Ask what the notes would show if a different person had conducted them.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A recall period longer than the memory can carry
questions.learningObjective: explain why a long-recall estimate and a short-recall count are not two measurements of one thing

stimulus.kind: interview schedule written for this question
stimulus.body: Interview schedule written for this exercise. 'Q3. Thinking back over the whole of last year, roughly how many times did you visit the reading room? Q4. And thinking back to last Tuesday, how many times did you visit it that day? The researcher's notes record 11 as the commonest answer to Q3, 0 as the commonest answer to Q4, and note that no respondent asked how the two questions were meant to relate.'

questions.stem: What does the difference between the two answers show?

options.text: That an annual estimate and a daily count are produced differently, so the two figures answer two questions
That the daily count is the more accurate one, since a single day is easier to recall than a year
options.misconception: treats ease of recall as accuracy, where the two questions are about different intervals

options.text: That 11 is the better estimate, since it came from a longer period of reflection on the habit
options.misconception: credits reflection with accuracy, which is the process that distorts a long estimate

options.text: That the two questions measure the same quantity and the gap shows the members were inattentive
options.misconception: assumes a common quantity and blames the respondents for the difference the design produced

questions.explanation: A year is reconstructed rather than recalled. Respondents answer Q3 by finding a few memorable occasions, multiplying them up, and rounding, which is a reasonable way to answer the question and a poor way to measure visits. Q4 is read off a specific day, and a member who came once on a Tuesday will say one and a member who did not will say none. The two figures are therefore not competing estimates of one number, and neither being larger than the other shows anything. The useful move is to use the short-recall question repeatedly across a sample of days and add up, which is more work and yields a number with a known basis, and to report the long-recall figure separately as a description of how members talk about the year.
questions.hint: Ask how a respondent produces a year of visits, and how many occasions they can actually name.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An answer that reports understanding rather than experience
questions.learningObjective: identify the ambiguity in a bare assent to a question about one's own experience
questions.stem: A member is asked whether the group's notice is easy to find, answers yes, and the interviewer moves to the next question. What has the reply established?

options.text: That the member found the notice easy to find, since a yes to a question about ease is about ease
options.misconception: takes a bare assent for a verdict on the member's experience, which is what the design cannot deliver

options.text: That the member did not experience a difficulty, since no difficulty was reported at that point
options.misconception: reads a silence after yes as an absence of difficulty, which is a different thing

options.text: That the reply is ambiguous, since assent can be a verdict on the experience or a way past the question
That the notice is easy to find, since one member's reply is a report about the notice itself
options.misconception: promotes a single assent to a fact about a document, which the design cannot support

questions.explanation: A bare yes to a question about one's own experience carries at least two things: a verdict on the experience, and a signal that the question was understood and is now over. The interview cannot tell which it got, and the asymmetry is the useful part, since a member who means no has to supply a reason and a member who means yes does not. So a yes is worth much less than a no, and the interviewer who wanted to know about the notice had a better question available: ask what the member did the last time they wanted to see the notice, or ask them to say where it is. The other three options each pick one of the two possible readings and report it as settled, which is the thing about a bare assent that no amount of analysis can repair afterwards.
questions.hint: Ask what a member would have to add if they meant no, and notice that a yes requires nothing.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A description of a practice and the practice itself
questions.learningObjective: state what a set of routine descriptions is evidence of
questions.stem: Asked how room booking is actually done, every member describes a step-by-step routine with named people. A member says the answers settle what the booking process is. What has the group got?

options.text: A set of descriptions rather than a process, so no group could learn a routine by asking
options.misconception: draws the opposite and equally wrong conclusion, that asking can never reach a practice

options.text: A majority account, since three members describing a routine the same way makes that the routine
options.misconception: counts agreement as confirmation, where a shared account can be a shared ideal

options.text: A set of accounts of a routine, which is one kind of evidence about it and not the whole of it
The booking process, since the people who do a routine weekly are the best witnesses to it
options.misconception: agrees that testimony is good evidence and then stops short of what it is evidence of

questions.explanation: Members describing a routine the same way is good evidence and the natural start of an enquiry into it, and it is not the same as having observed the routine. A description can be the official account, the account a member believes to be current, the account that omits the workaround everyone uses, or the account a member gives to a newcomer. Each is worth having and each needs something else beside it. The cheap checks are unremarkable: ask what happened the last time it went differently, ask the person at the far end of the chain, ask a new member what they were told, and compare the description against the artefacts, which for a booking system means the sheet. The fourth option is the tempting over-read and the first is its mirror, and a group that concludes it can never learn a practice by asking has lost the cheapest instrument it has.
questions.hint: Ask what the description leaves out, and who would be in a position to know.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Asking about a job instead of about a routine
questions.learningObjective: recognise the question whose wording invites a general account
questions.stem: An interviewer asks a long-serving member how the group's intake works, and is answered with an account of what the job involves. What is the likeliest reason?

options.text: The member chose the general account because a general account is the easier one to be right about
options.misconception: supposes a strategic choice by the member, where the wording does the steering

options.text: The member knows the job better than the intake routine, since intake was always another part's work
options.misconception: converts a question about wording into a claim about what the member knows

options.text: The interviewer spoke too quickly, so the member answered the question the interviewer appeared to ask
options.misconception: locates the fault in delivery, which the transcript of the question as recorded does not support

options.text: The question asked about the job, and an account of the job is what the question as worded invited

questions.explanation: How does the job work is a question about the job, and the member has answered it well. A routine is a sequence of particular acts by particular people, and a question has to ask for that shape or the account will not have it: what happened the last time someone rang, who did what, in what order, and where the paperwork went. The useful discovery here is that the instrument produced a coherent but wrong-kind of answer, which is a more common failure than a bad answer and is easier to miss. The second and third options each move the problem to the member rather than to the schedule, and the fourth invents a delivery fault, when the transcript shows the question the interviewer actually put and it is the question that is at fault.
questions.hint: Ask what shape of answer the wording of the question permits, and what shape the group wanted.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An account and a record that disagree
questions.learningObjective: state what an account and a record are each evidence of when they conflict
questions.stem: A member says the reading room closed early on 14 evenings last term. The booking sheet shows 22 evenings ending at 6 pm and one ending at 9 pm. The member works from a habit of arriving at 6. Four positions follow. Which is the strongest supported judgement?

options.text: The two are about different thresholds, so the counts differ without either record being wrong
The member is right and the sheet is wrong, since someone present each evening knows what happened
options.misconception: settles the conflict by proximity, which is a fact about the witness and not about the evenings

options.text: The sheet is right and the member is wrong, since a written record settles a question of fact
options.misconception: gives the written record a standing the disagreement has not yet established for it

options.text: Both are right, since a room can close early and a booking can run to 9 pm in the same evening
options.misconception: describes a possibility without addressing the 14 against 22 that is the actual disagreement

questions.explanation: The two records are counting against different thresholds, and that is the whole of the disagreement. The member treats 6 pm as the closing time and therefore counts an evening as early-closed when they arrive and find it shut; the sheet records 22 evenings that ended at 6 pm, and a member who arrived on 14 of those 22 has counted 14 without contradicting anybody. Both records are sound and they answer different questions. What the group should do is fix the definition, since it now has a real example of why the group's own attendance figures need one: was a member present at the close, or present at 6 pm, or present for any part of the evening. The fourth option describes a thing that could be true and does not address the numbers, and the second and third each pick a winner by a rule the group has not established.
questions.hint: Ask what counts as early, and when each of the two records was counting from.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The respondents who answered were the wrong ones
questions.learningObjective: identify a response set whose composition argues against generalising from it

stimulus.kind: memorandum written for this question
stimulus.body: Memorandum written for this exercise. 'Members were asked whether the new marking schedule is an improvement. A long-serving member who had helped write the schedule replied that it clearly is. Two members who had objected to the schedule when it was proposed did not reply at all. The memo reports the response as unanimous support and recommends the schedule be adopted for the following year.'

questions.stem: What is the strongest objection to the memo's use of the responses?

options.text: The two silent members may simply have had no view, so the silence supports the memo's finding
options.misconception: reaches for a benign account of a silence that two prior objections already explain

options.text: The one who replied helped write it and the two who objected are silent, so the replies are not a sample of members
The memo should have asked every member twice, since one reply from each is a thin basis for a report
options.misconception: proposes repetition, which would have returned the same single reply from the same person

options.text: The member who replied cannot be neutral, and no member is neutral about a rule they helped write
options.misconception: makes neutrality the standard, which would disqualify testimony from anyone involved at all

questions.explanation: Who replied is the finding here, and the memo's reply is exactly the person for whom an affirmative answer costs nothing, while the two members known to have a contrary view did not answer at all. So the memo has learned that one supporter and one author replied, and it has reported this as unanimity among members, which it is not. A non-response that correlates with a view is evidence about the population, and the remedy is small: report the response rate, go and ask the two, and put the two accounts side by side in the recommendation. The third option is a procedural refinement that would not have produced a different reply, the fourth option sets a standard of neutrality that would empty the record of anyone involved, and the first option reaches for the most charitable account of a silence that has an obvious explanation two lines earlier in the same memo.
questions.hint: Ask who replied, and what the memo already says about the members who did not.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A member's account of why a rule was applied as it was
questions.learningObjective: state what such an account is evidence of and how to use it next
questions.stem: A member says the reason the group's late submissions rose is that the new cap was applied strictly. First say what the member's account is evidence of, then say how the group should use it. What must the first answer contain?

options.text: That the cap caused the rise, since the member is the one who had to live with the practice of it
options.misconception: confuses standing to report an experience with evidence that the experience was caused by it

options.text: That the member is mistaken, since members do not administer the policies they are asked about
options.misconception: dismisses the account on grounds of role, where the role is what makes it worth having

options.text: That the member believes strict application caused the rise, since an account of a reason is not a record of one
That the cap was applied strictly, since the member was present for every discussion of the cap
options.misconception: treats presence at discussions as observation of their application, which is elsewhere

questions.explanation: The account is good evidence of what the member believes and of the experience that produced the belief, which is a real contribution: someone who was making late submissions under the cap knows what the cap felt like and may know of cases. It is not a record of the cap's application, and the difference matters because the second stage turns on it. The group can test the member's belief against records it can reach: submissions by week against the weeks when the cap was tightened, the number of extensions granted, whether the increase is among the members who submit often enough to hit a cap, and what the two members who objected at the time said. The other three options each collapse belief into fact in one direction or the other, and the last is the one a seminar is most likely to reach for, since dismissing a member's account is easier than testing it.
questions.hint: Ask what the account is a record of, and what the group could look at to check it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An interview record that shows only what was written down
questions.learningObjective: state what a thin transcript supports and what it leaves unrecoverable

stimulus.kind: interview extract written for this question
stimulus.body: Interview extract written for this exercise. 'Q2. What did you do when the system refused your request? A. Tried again the next morning. Q3. Anything else? A. Nothing. Interviewer's note: the member paused for several seconds at this point and then said nothing further. The interview ran for 34 minutes. The transcript of this interview, in full, is 11 words, and the schedule records 26 questions, of which 4 were put.'

questions.stem: What can the group take from this record?

options.text: Two answers and a note about a silence, and the silence is not a finding about the member
That the member had nothing further to add, since an open question was put and nothing came back
options.misconception: reads a single open slot as the whole interview, when 22 of the 26 questions were not put

options.text: That the record cannot be used, since 11 words cannot carry the weight of a 34-minute interview
options.misconception: discards the part of the record that is accurate in order to avoid reporting the rest

options.text: That the member was reluctant throughout, since a pause before saying nothing shows reluctance
options.misconception: treats one ambiguous pause as a settled disposition, when the note records an impression

questions.explanation: The record is accurate as far as it goes: two answers were given, four of 26 questions were put, and the member said nothing further to the question that invited it. What the group cannot get is the other 33 minutes, and the reason is a procedural failure it can see: four questions out of 26, transcribed to 11 words. The pause is an impression written by the interviewer in the same document as the answers, which is a bad arrangement because a later reader cannot easily separate what was said from what was thought. The repair is to keep a running note during the interview, to record which questions were and were not put, and to hold silences apart from answers. The fourth option is the tempting one, and a pause before nothing is equally consistent with thinking, with a question that did not apply, and with a member who has said what they came to say.
questions.hint: Ask how many of the scheduled questions were actually put, and where the impressions are recorded.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Choosing which sessions to observe
questions.learningObjective: identify a sample of the observer's own choosing when the choice may bear on the outcome
questions.stem: A member observes four of the group's own sessions to write about how decisions are made. In the four observed, decisions took 22 minutes on average, against 31 minutes in the two sessions not observed. What is the likeliest explanation of the gap?

options.text: The member's presence shortened the sessions, so the observer is part of what was measured
options.misconception: supplies the observer effect, which usually points the other way and is not separable here

options.text: The member timed the observed sessions differently, and one observer's counts are thin evidence
options.misconception: raises a real but secondary point without touching how the sessions were selected

options.text: Two sessions cannot be compared with four, so the gap carries no information either way
options.misconception: dismisses the comparison on size where the problem is which sessions made up each group

options.text: The member chose which sessions to attend, so the choice may bear on how long the sessions ran

questions.explanation: The member chose the sample, and a member choosing four of six sessions is likely to choose the ones that interest them, which may well be the settled ones. That is a hypothesis rather than a verdict, and it is testable in the cheapest way available: the member should list which sessions they expect to attend before looking at how long any of them ran, and the comparison should be made against the timetable rather than against two remembered evenings. The first option is a real and important effect, and it points the wrong way for this result, since an extra person in the room more often lengthens deliberation than shortens it. The member's own timing is worth checking too, and two sessions is a thin comparison; but the selection is the explanation that would change what the group writes, so it is the one to reach first.
questions.hint: Ask how the four sessions were chosen, and what the member would have chosen to write about.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A verbatim record and a cleaned-up one
questions.learningObjective: identify what a cleaned transcription removes and what it therefore cannot be used for

stimulus.kind: two transcriptions written for this question
stimulus.body: Two transcriptions of one recorded turn, written for this exercise. The recording is heard as: a member um the uh form no it was no just the form. Verbatim transcription, as the recorder hears it: 'a member um the uh form no it was no just the form'. Cleaned-up transcription: 'A member said no, it was just the form.' The transcriber's cover note reads: cleaned up for readability, fillers and false starts removed, and no other change made.

questions.stem: What does the pair of transcriptions show?

options.text: The two disagree about the speaker's position, so the group must choose between them on evidence
options.misconception: turns a transcription decision into a factual dispute the recording cannot settle for anyone

options.text: The cleaned version is easier to read and has dropped the places where the speaker changed direction
The verbatim version is unusable for analysis, since fillers carry no meaning for the argument
options.misconception: dismisses the only version that records what was actually said at each point

options.text: The cleaned version is the honest one, since it reports what the speaker was trying to say
options.misconception: makes intention the standard for a transcript, which cannot be read off the recording

That decision is defensible for some purposes and fatal for others. A claim about what the room argued needs the reversals, since an argument that changed direction is not the argument that was announced. A claim about what a member believed at the end of the turn is better served by the cleaned version, because that is what the cleaning preserved. Draft the open questions before the fixed ones, since a fixed question closes the answer the open one was for

options.misconception: over-corrects, and would leave the group with no record of the quiet or the remark at all

options.text: A finding, since a pattern across sessions of this kind is a result a group can rely on
options.misconception: promotes one session to a pattern, which is what six sessions would be needed to begin

options.text: Things seen, an interpretation of them, and one utterance, and only some of it can be checked later

questions.stem: What does the report's own arithmetic show about the 400 per cent figure?

options.text: Complaints rose fivefold, which is a fivefold rise whatever the enquiries did in the same years
options.misconception: holds that a count is a rate, so any growth in the base is ignored by construction

options.text: Complaints fell, since 120 among 12,000 is a smaller share than 24 among 1,800
options.misconception: states the right direction while getting the share the wrong way round

options.text: The officer's figure is right, and 400 per cent is the only way to express a rise of that size
options.misconception: treats a percentage of a count as the whole finding, with the base left out of it

options.text: Complaints rose fivefold while enquiries rose about sevenfold, so the share of enquiries complaining fell

options.misconception: supposes exclusive use, which nothing in the instrument or the report states

options.misconception: demands one particular form, which is a house style rather than an arithmetic requirement

options.text: Both are consistent, since 0.8 per 1,000 is one fifth of 4.0 and one fifth of a figure is 20 per cent of it
The first is right and the second is wrong, since 20 per cent of 4.0 is 0.8 and the two are not the same measure

options.text: The second is right and the first is wrong, since a per cent change is the clearer way to report a fall
options.misconception: settles a question of presentation as though it were a question of correctness

The two conventions are different and both correct: a difference in rates is given in points so that a reader can see the size in the original units, and a per cent change is given as a ratio so that figures with different units can be compared. questions.topic: An average that most of the cases fall far below
questions.learningObjective: compute a mean and decide what it does and does not describe about the set

stimulus.kind: facilities report written for this question
stimulus.body: Facilities report written for this exercise. 'The mean time members spent in the reading room per visit was 17 minutes. The room plan seats 40 readers and assumes each stays 17 minutes, giving 680 reader-minutes a session. A separate count of 100 visits in the same period gives: 60 visits of 5 minutes, 25 visits of 20 minutes, and 15 visits of 60 minutes. The report gives no other breakdown and says the 15 long visits were mostly the same eight members.'

questions.stem: What does the count show about the figure the plan is built on?

options.text: The mean of 17 is right and the plan is safe, since an average cannot be exceeded by most visits
options.misconception: assumes a mean describes the typical case, which is what a bimodal set denies

options.text: The mean of 17 is right, and the 15 long visits show a few members would fill the room alone
options.misconception: reads a true observation as the answer, while leaving the plan's own assumption unexamined

options.text: The mean of 17 is right, and 60 of 100 visits were 5 minutes, so the plan's typical visit is the exception
The mean of 17 is wrong, since 60 of the 100 visits were 5 minutes and no average can sit that high
options.misconception: treats the most common value as the average, which is a different statistic altogether

What the mean does not do is describe a typical visit, because the set is not clustered around its own average. Six visits in ten were 5 minutes, the median visit is 5 minutes, and 17 minutes is not a value any of the hundred visits had. A plan that seats 40 readers and multiplies by 17 is therefore planning for a visit that is not the ordinary one, and the figure for the ordinary one is 5. The fourth option is the commonest error about means and it is a confusion with the mode; the first option takes the mean to be typical, which is exactly the assumption the plan rests on; and the second option is a true observation about the eight members, which is worth knowing and is not the question the plan has to answer.

stimulus.body: Pilot evaluation written for this exercise, on a marking support session run in two halls. Hall B, which took most of its students from a course with a low prior attainment rate: 1 of 10 who attended passed, against 1 of 20 who did not. Pooled across both halls, 10 of 20 who attended passed and 90 of 120 who did not. The evaluation reports the pooled figure: attendance at the session was associated with a pass rate of 50 per cent against 75 per cent, and concludes that the session did not help and should be withdrawn.'

questions.stem: What does the evaluation's own table show about the conclusion?

options.text: Attendance is ahead in both halls, and the pooled figure reverses a pattern the hall figures agree on
The pooled figure is the right one, since pooling is what removes the differences between the halls
options.misconception: treats aggregation as correction, which is the step that produces the reversal

options.text: The pooled figure is the right one, since the halls differ in size and the larger hall should count for more
options.misconception: proposes weighting by size, which is precisely what the pooled figure already does

options.text: The halls differ so much that nothing in the table bears on the session at all
options.misconception: dismisses the table wholesale, where the hall figures agree and are readable

Both statements are true of the numbers they describe, and the pooling is what produces the reversal, because the two halls' pass rates are so different that the pooled denominator is dominated by Hall A's non-attenders. The conclusion drawn from the pooled figure is therefore not available. The interesting fact is the one the table hides: the session appears to help in the hall where it works and not in the hall where the base rate is low, and that is a question worth a seminar rather than a reason to withdraw anything.
questions.hint: Work out each hall's two rates on their own, and only then the two pooled rates.

questions.topic: What a screen's good rate is measured against
questions.learningObjective: compute what a positive result is worth once the frequency of the condition is in the table

stimulus.body: Screening table written for this exercise, for a short suitability screen used before a placement. '1,000 applicants were screened. 100 were later confirmed unsuitable and 900 were confirmed suitable. The screen flagged 100 applicants. Of the 100 flagged, 10 were among those confirmed unsuitable and 90 were among those confirmed suitable. Of the 100 confirmed unsuitable, 10 had been flagged. A note records that the flagging rate is reported in the service handbook as 90 per cent accurate.'

questions.stem: What does the table show about the handbook's 90 per cent figure?

options.text: The figure is sound, since 90 of the 100 applicants flagged were confirmed suitable by the later check
options.misconception: reads a conditional on the wrong population, since the 90 are a count within the flags

options.text: The figure should be 10 per cent, since the screen catches one unsuitable applicant in ten
options.misconception: reads the same coverage in the other direction and calls it an accuracy where it is a rate

options.text: The figure shows the screen is unfair to suitable applicants, since 90 of them were flagged and cleared
options.misconception: turns a question of interpretation into a claim about fairness, which the table cannot decide

options.text: Of the 100 flags, 90 concern suitable applicants, since only 1 unsuitable applicant in 10 is ever flagged

questions.explanation: The handbook has taken a proportion computed among the flagged and presented it as the screen's accuracy. Of the 100 flagged, 10 were unsuitable and 90 were suitable, which is true and is a statement about the composition of the flags. The number that matters for someone who has been flagged is that only 1 in 10 of the unsuitable applicants was caught: 10 of the 100 confirmed unsuitable were flagged, so 90 slipped through. Someone reading the handbook's figure would conclude that a flag is nearly always a false alarm, and that inference does not follow, because a flag being a false alarm most of the time is exactly what a service that is flagging 100 of 1,000 applicants will produce when the condition is rare. The useful figures for the handbook are the 100 flags out of 1,000, the 10 of 100 unsuitable caught, and the 90 of 1,000 suitable flagged.
questions.hint: Ask what a flagged applicant wants to know, and find the rate that answers that question.

options.misconception: assumes a publication date settles the tense of a figure inside the text

questions.topic: More decimal places than the instrument can support
questions.learningObjective: identify implied precision that the measuring procedure cannot deliver

stimulus.kind: protocol note written for this question
stimulus.body: Protocol note written for this exercise, for a study of marking time. 'The mean marking time per script was 12.476 minutes, n = 212. The protocol specifies that the stopwatch is read to the nearest second and started when the marker turns the first page. Two observers independently timed 12 of the same scripts and their readings differed by up to 9 seconds on the same script, which the protocol treats as the expected disagreement between two readers.'

questions.stem: What is the difficulty with the figure as reported?

options.text: A stopwatch read to the second cannot support a mean given to thousandths, so the extra places are not in the data
Three decimal places are needed for a mean of that size, and 212 scripts is more than enough to supply them
options.misconception: assumes averaging manufactures precision the instrument never recorded, which it cannot

options.text: The extra places show the timing was done carefully, and care is what makes a measurement precise
options.misconception: equates care with resolution, which are separate properties of a measurement

options.text: The mean should carry two places, since three is more decimal places than the protocol permits
options.misconception: invents a house rule, where the protocol fixes the reading and not the number of places reported

questions.explanation: Averaging a hundred readings each good to a second gives a mean that is itself good to a small fraction of a second, and it does not give a mean good to a thousandth of a minute. The extra places are produced by the arithmetic, not measured, and a reader who sees 12.476 minutes will believe something is known to a twenty-fourth of a second that nobody recorded. The two observers disagreeing by up to 9 seconds on the same script says the same thing from the other direction, and it is a stronger piece of evidence than the printed figure, since it comes from the protocol. The second option is the mistake that makes this worth teaching: a large sample improves the reliability of a mean without improving the resolution of the instrument behind it. The last option invents a rule the protocol does not contain.
questions.hint: Ask how precisely one reading was made, and what averaging can and cannot add to that.

stimulus.body: Three-year summary written for this exercise. 'Complaint resolution within 5 working days was 78 per cent in each of the three years. A note in the third year's file reads: from April of the third year the office began counting requests arriving through the online channel as complaints, having previously counted them as requests handled elsewhere. The three years' figures of 156, 195, and 390 are the counts resolved in time, and the office reports the rate as unchanged over the period.'

questions.stem: What does the note do to the claim that resolution did not change?

options.text: It adds a class of request to the third year's complaints, so the three rates are over different populations
It changes a definition once, and a single change cannot affect a trend across three years
options.misconception: understates what a change in the counted population does to a rate in the year it occurs

options.text: It shows the office improved its counting, which makes the later rate the more accurate of the three
options.misconception: confuses a better record with a comparable one, and the two are not the same thing

options.text: It shows the base grew through the period, and a growing base cancels any change in the rate
options.misconception: invokes a size effect where the note describes a change in what was counted at all

questions.explanation: The arithmetic is all correct: 156 of 200, 195 of 250, and 390 of 500 are each 78 per cent. What the note changes is what those rates are rates of. From April of the third year the complaint count includes a class of request it previously excluded, so the third year's 78 per cent is the share of a larger, differently composed population that was resolved in time, and the two earlier years are shares of the old one. A series that is flat because the thing being counted changed is a series that cannot be described as steady. The group's next step is not to distrust the arithmetic but to ask for the third year's count on the old definition, which the office should be able to produce and which would settle how much of the continuity is real.

options.misconception: claims a precision an index does not have, since it rescales the same two numbers

options.text: On the choice of 2020 as the endpoint, since a different final year would give a different figure
options.misconception: makes the endpoint the variable when the endpoint is fixed in the note and the base is not

options.text: On which year was set to 100, since the two endpoint counts also give about 34 per cent on a 2015 base

The projection is sound, since a rise of 45 per cent a year doubles any base within the five years given

options.text: The bars are drawn from the foot, so the chart shows a rise and any doubt is only about how it is labelled

options.text: The axis starts at 20, so a rise of 3 fills well over a third of the chart and looks bigger

stimulus.body: Two-service comparison written for this exercise. 'Hospital A recorded 12 complaints in the year and treated 400 patients. options.text: A is the better service, since 12 is a third of 36 and the comparison is a like for like
options.misconception: compares counts while leaving out that the two hospitals saw different numbers of patients

options.text: Neither figure can be used, since the two populations differ and every comparison between them is unfair
options.misconception: draws the right caution and applies it as a total refusal, which is not what the numbers require

options.text: B is worse only if its patients complain more readily, which nobody has measured at either hospital
options.misconception: states a real limitation and treats it as the answer, leaving the arithmetic uncomputed

options.misconception: invents a direction of effect that the note does not supply either way

options.text: The figures are not comparable and the series should be withdrawn, since a changed definition voids a rate
options.misconception: over-corrects, treating a disclosure about the count as a reason to suppress the figures

The third assigns a direction to the change without any basis for it, since adding requests can raise or lower a rate depending on how those requests fare. That the two means are of different things, since a mean before and after a rule cannot be compared
options.misconception: supposes the two means are incommensurable, which is what a before-and-after comparison is for

options.text: That a fall of 7 minutes is too large to have come from a triage rule, so the figures must be wrong

options.misconception: accepts a comparison whose base is unknown, which is the gap the objection is about

stimulus.kind: reading-room log written for this question
stimulus.body: Reading-room log written for this exercise, for one week. 'Sign-ins by day: Monday 18, Tuesday 22, Wednesday 9, Thursday 24, Friday 11. Total for the week 84. The room seats 30. questions.stem: Which two of the four drafted statements does the log support?

options.text: The mean is 16.8, and it is not the number of sign-ins on any one day of the week
The room's capacity of 30 was exceeded on two days of the week
options.misconception: confuses the highest day with the capacity, and the highest day is 24 against a capacity of 30

options.text: The median day of the week had 18 sign-ins
Wednesday's 9 was less than half of the mean of 16.8 sign-ins
options.misconception: compares 9 with half of 16.8, which is 8.4, and so gets the comparison backwards

questions.explanation: The five days are 18, 22, 9, 24, and 11, which total 84, so the mean is 84 over 5, or 16.8, and no day had exactly that number, which is ordinary for a mean over five values and is what the first statement says. All four are the kind of statement a group produces when the numbers are in front of it and nobody has divided anything.
questions.hint: Add the five numbers, divide by five, and then put the five in order to find the middle one.

questions.learningObjective: state what a group may claim about a past event that left no record
questions.stem: A member reports that in 1988 the group's intake rule was changed without a minute. The 1988 papers do not survive and everyone involved has left. First say what the group may claim, then say how to write it. What must the first answer contain?

options.text: That the rule was changed, since a member who remembers it is better evidence than a file nobody has
options.misconception: converts a report into a finding, which is the step the missing record was supposed to justify

options.text: That nothing may be claimed, since a rule with no documentation must be treated as never having existed
options.misconception: makes an evidential limit into a rule about what may be said, and erases the group's own past

options.text: That the claim holds if enough members remember it, so the group should ask every member still in post
options.misconception: proposes a vote, where more agreeing witnesses from the same circle add little independence

options.text: That a member's report is the evidence there is, so the group can report the report and name it as one source

questions.explanation: A group with one eyewitness and no paperwork has one eyewitness, and the honest sentence is of the form: a member reports that the 1988 intake rule was changed without a minute, and no 1988 papers survive to confirm or contradict this. That sentence is usable, and a reader can weigh it. The first option is the slide the item is about, since the memory has become the fact and the missing file has been quietly promoted to a standard it cannot meet. The second is the opposite error, in which a limit on the evidence becomes a prohibition on the record, and the third option mistakes agreement for independence, because members who worked together in 1988 share the same conversations and the same accounts. The remaining step is to look for the artefact the rule would have left behind, which may still exist in a form nobody has thought of as a record.
questions.hint: Ask what the group holds, and what a reader could be told that would be true whatever happened in 1988.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A transcript whose recording nobody holds
questions.learningObjective: state what a machine-made transcript can and cannot be checked against
questions.stem: A group has a transcript made by an automated service. Nobody holds the audio, the service's settings, or the version of the software that produced it. What follows?

options.text: That the transcript is void, since a record nobody can re-observe may never be used in a discussion
options.misconception: excludes the record entirely, when a group may still reason from it with its limits named

options.text: That the transcript is sound throughout, since a machine had no motive to alter what it heard
options.misconception: assumes accuracy from the absence of motive, and never considers how the service operates

options.text: That the transcript may be used only for the number of speakers, which the service counts without an audio file
options.misconception: invents one narrow use the service has not been shown to support better than anything else

options.text: That the transcript cannot be checked against the audio, so a disputed word rests on the service's reliability alone

questions.explanation: A transcript is a claim about a recording, and this group cannot put the two side by side, so every disputed word has the service as its only witness. That is a real weakness and it is a specific one, which means it can be handled: the group should use the transcript for the structure of what was said, treat any wording that matters as provisional, and look for whatever else records the same meeting, since a member's own notes would settle a dispute that the transcript cannot. The first option throws away the most complete record the group has, and the second option confuses the absence of a motive to deceive with an assurance of accuracy, when the usual failures are technical rather than dishonest. The fourth invents a use the group has no evidence the service performs well.
questions.hint: Ask what a transcript is a claim about, and whether the group can check that claim.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An account that conflicts with a record and must appear beside it
questions.learningObjective: select the reporting form that keeps a conflict visible rather than resolving it silently
questions.stem: A group holds a rota sheet recording who changed a shift and when, and a member's account that the change was made verbally by a senior member. The sheet names no one. Four ways of reporting the two follow. Which is the strongest supported judgement?

options.text: Report the sheet and the account side by side, since each speaks to a different part of what happened
Report the account, since a sheet that names nobody cannot be tested and a person can be asked
options.misconception: prefers the checkable account on the ground that the sheet is untestable, which is not its defect

options.text: Report the sheet, since a contemporaneous record outranks any later account of the same matter
options.misconception: grants the sheet a standing the member's account contests and the group has not settled

options.text: Report neither, since the group cannot say which is right and a conflict cannot be printed
options.misconception: assumes a printed record must settle the question, when its use is to show the reader what is at stake

questions.explanation: The two records answer different questions and neither contradicts the other. The sheet says a shift changed at a time and the sheet's rule for recording names nobody, which is a fact about the sheet; the account says the change came verbally from a senior member, which is a fact about how it came about. Printed side by side with a line saying the two were not reconciled, a reader can see exactly what is known and what is missing, and a later group can pick the work up. The second and third options both resolve the conflict by a rule of standing, and neither rule is available: a sheet is not uncheckable because it omits names, and an account is not inferior because it is later. The fourth is the one a nervous group reaches for, and it gives the reader nothing, since a report that says two things conflict and prints neither has hidden the conflict rather than recorded it.
questions.hint: Ask what each record is a record of, and whether the two are actually in conflict at all.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Reconciling an account with a record in order
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of reconciling two sources so each depends on the one before
questions.stem: A group holds a record and an account that do not agree. Put the steps in the order that lets each depend on the one before it.

options.text: State what each source is a record of, since two records of different acts may not conflict at all
Fix the rules each source used, since a rule left unstated is a standing conflict waiting to happen
Look for the part of the disagreement that survives both accounts, since that is what can be reported
Report the agreed part and the open part in separate sentences, since a reader needs both

questions.explanation: The first two steps are what stop a group reconciling two things that were never in conflict. A record and an account often disagree because one counts members and the other counts meetings, or because a sheet records a change and a person remembers a conversation, and a group that reads a disagreement before it has asked what each source is a record of will spend the discussion settling something nobody disputed. Only once the acts and the rules are fixed can the group find what survives both, which is the part it can report with confidence. The report comes last and it is two sentences, not one: what both sources support, and what remains open. An alternative order that puts the reporting step third leaves the reader with a claim nobody has checked, and one that puts the rules before the acts has the group deciding conventions without knowing what they are conventions about.
questions.hint: Ask which step, done out of order, leaves the ones after it with nothing to reconcile.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Which statements a mixed record will support
questions.learningObjective: select the claims a mixed record supports and reject the ones it does not

stimulus.kind: seminar record written for this question
stimulus.body: Seminar record written for this exercise. 'Three interviews were conducted with members about a rota, and a booking sheet for the period was obtained from the office. One of the three interviewees was a member of the committee that had written the rota. Four statements were drafted for the report. Statement 1: the committee member's account is a first-hand account of a decision they took part in. Statement 2: the three interviews are three independent accounts, and their agreement establishes what the practice is. Statement 3: the booking sheet gives 22 evenings, and 22 is what the report states for the period. Statement 4: the practice is well understood by members, since three interviewees agreed about it.'

questions.stem: Which two of the four drafted statements does the record support?

options.text: The committee member's account is a first-hand account of a decision they took part in
The three interviews are three independent accounts, and their agreement establishes the practice
options.misconception: counts the three as independent when one interviewee helped write what they describe

options.text: The booking sheet gives 22 evenings, and 22 is what the report states for the period
The practice is well understood by members, since three interviewees agreed about it
options.misconception: reads agreement among three as a property of the practice, which no number of accounts establishes

questions.explanation: Two of the four statements are reportable as written. The committee member was present for the decision being described, so their account is first-hand for that decision, and saying so is a claim the record carries. The sheet gives 22 evenings and the group holds the sheet, so 22 is a figure the group can state. The other two fail on the same underlying move, which is turning a small number of accounts into a property of the practice. The three interviews are not independent, since one of the three helped write the rota, and even if they were, agreement among three people does not establish what a practice is; it establishes what three people said. The fourth statement is the version of the error that gets published, because it sounds modest and is really a generalisation from a handful of accounts with the count left out.
questions.hint: Ask which statements report something the group holds, and which generalise from it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a record with interviews and meetings in it will support
questions.learningObjective: state the strongest claim a mixed record of interviews and meetings carries
questions.stem: A seminar's record for one term holds 18 meeting logs and 14 interviews, with a note that 3 of the 14 interviewees were on the committee that designed the scheme under discussion. Four readings of what the seminar may claim follow. Which is the strongest supported judgement?

options.text: That the record supports nothing, since three of the fourteen were involved and the rest cannot be trusted
options.misconception: discards eleven accounts because three are compromised, which is a different claim

options.text: That the record supports a claim about what members in general think, since most interviewees were not on the committee
options.misconception: promotes a majority of a small sample into what members in general think

options.text: That the record supports a description of the 11 other interviewees' accounts, and not a claim about the practice
That the record supports a claim about the scheme, since 14 interviews and 18 meeting logs is a thorough enquiry
options.misconception: measures thoroughness by volume, which is not what decides what a record shows

questions.explanation: The record supports a description of what 11 people who were not on the committee said, reported as what those 11 said, and it does not support a claim about the practice or about what members in general think. That is a real result and it is worth more than the version the group would prefer, because a reader can see who was asked, who was not, and what the record leaves out. The fourth option mistakes the amount of material for its scope, which is a common way a thorough-looking file is mistaken for a thorough enquiry. The first is the over-correction that throws away eleven accounts because three are compromised, and it is also wrong about the arithmetic of compromise, since the three are described separately. The fourth is the sentence that gets published by accident: a majority of fourteen is not what members in general think, and the word in general is doing all the work.
questions.hint: Ask how many accounts the group can describe, and what a description of accounts is not.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Getting from one member's account to a claim about a practice
questions.learningObjective: state what a group would need before calling one person's account the practice
questions.stem: A member describes in detail how a late submission reaches a marker. First say what the description supports, then say what the group would need before calling it the practice. What must the second answer contain?

options.text: The member's agreement that the description is accurate, since the member is the person who does the work
options.misconception: asks the describer to certify the claim, which adds no evidence the group did not have

options.text: A second description from the same member a month later, since repetition shows the account is stable
options.misconception: repeats one source, which cannot check the source it repeats

options.text: A tally of how many submissions travel that route, since only a count can establish a practice
options.misconception: supplies prevalence where the group needs the route itself, and misses the other steps entirely

options.text: Accounts from members at other points in the chain, and a check against the records the submissions leave

questions.explanation: A detailed account from the person who does the work is good evidence about their part of the work, and the second stage is about extending it. The group needs the other points in the chain, since a process has at least a sender and a receiver and one person's account cannot settle what happens after their part, and it needs the artefacts, because a timestamp, a receipt, and a marking log will show whether the route the member describes is the route submissions take. The third option is the instructive error: a tally would establish how common a route is, which is a different question, and it would still not tell the group what the route is. A group that wants to know both should ask the chain and then count, in that order, and should not confuse the second result for the first.
questions.hint: Ask who else handles a submission after this member, and what the submissions themselves leave behind.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Two replies that are one reply
questions.learningObjective: identify duplicated replies in a set of accounts and correct the count

stimulus.kind: memorandum written for this question
stimulus.body: Memorandum written for this exercise. 'Four members were asked to describe how the rota is built, and four replies were received. Two of the four had the conversation together, and their two replies match in every particular, including the phrase we was about to give her. The other two replies are distinct from each other and from that pair. The memo reports four accounts of how the rota is built and concludes that the practice is widely understood among the members asked.'

questions.stem: What should the group make of the four accounts?

options.text: They are three accounts rather than four, and the agreement is narrower than the memo reports it as being
They are four accounts, since each member wrote a reply and each reply is a separate piece of evidence
options.misconception: counts the acts of writing rather than the accounts, and misses what the match shows

options.text: The pair should be dropped, since a matched pair of replies shows the practice is not widely held
options.misconception: turns a duplication into a refutation, which is the opposite of what duplication shows

options.text: The shared phrase shows the rota is built by a fixed script, which the group may now report
options.misconception: reads one idiom as a documented procedure, which is a very different kind of claim

questions.explanation: Two replies matching in every particular, including a shared phrase, are one account written twice, so the group holds three accounts and not four, and the agreement is one pair's rather than four people's. That is a smaller basis than the memo reports, and the correction should go into the memo rather than being noted privately. The fourth option is the tempting inference and it shows how far a single shared phrase can be pushed: people who worked together talk alike, and an idiom is not a written procedure. The second option is the counting error the match exposes, and the third is the opposite mistake, in which a duplicate is read as a contradiction. What the group can still say is that three accounts, one of them shared by two members, describe the rota, and it can say how many of the members asked were involved in the conversation.
questions.hint: Ask how many separate conversations produced the four replies.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A witness who is also a party to what is described
questions.learningObjective: state what a file establishes when two accounts agree and no approval is recorded

stimulus.kind: file extract written for this question
stimulus.body: Extract from a file, written for this exercise. 'Memorandum by the group's own adviser, dated 1974: the office was instructed to delay the notice by six weeks. I advised the delay and I accept now that it was wrong, since notice to staff is required by the standing orders. A second memorandum in the file, by the then secretary, states: the delay was at the chairman's verbal request and I acted on it. The file contains no minute of any meeting at which the delay was approved, and the file's index records two items for that quarter only, being these two memoranda.'

questions.stem: What can the group establish about why the notice was delayed?

options.text: That the standing orders were broken, since a delay of six weeks is longer than a standing order allows
options.misconception: invents a length limit that no standing order in the file supplies

options.text: That two people account for the delay in terms of an instruction, and the file records no approval of it
That the delay was authorised, since an adviser writing about it shows the office considered it properly
options.misconception: reads the existence of a memorandum about a decision as evidence that the decision was sound

options.text: That the chairman gave the instruction, since one document says so and the other does not deny it
options.misconception: treats an uncontradicted assertion as established, and the other document is silent

questions.explanation: The file establishes two things and leaves a third open. Two people say the delay came from an instruction, and the adviser accepts the delay was wrong, which is a concession by a participant with a reason to be careful. What the file does not contain is any minute approving the delay, and the index says the quarter's record is those two items, so the absence is in the record rather than in the search. The chairman is named in one document and not denied in the other, and that is a lead rather than a finding; the secretary was reporting what they were told. The group could put the two accounts side by side, state that no approval is recorded, and ask the office whether a minute exists elsewhere. The third option is the error this kind of file invites, since an uncontradicted statement is the weakest kind of evidence there is.
questions.hint: Ask what the file positively contains, and what its index says is missing from the quarter.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A practice generalised from one member's account of it
questions.learningObjective: identify the step from a detailed account to a claim about what most people do
questions.stem: One member describes in detail how bookings are made by telephone, adding that most callers ring rather than come in. Another member concludes the group should close the counter, since almost nobody uses it. What is the difficulty?

options.text: The account covers the telephone route and one member's habit, not how often each route is used overall
The member is the wrong witness, since a long-serving member knows less about bookings than the office does
options.misconception: objects to the witness on rank, where the problem is the kind of claim being made

options.text: The counter should close, since one member's detailed account is better evidence than a count
options.misconception: prefers the account to the count, when the two answer different questions entirely

options.text: There is no difficulty, since a detailed account is exactly what a generalisation needs and this one is detailed
options.misconception: treats detail as coverage, which is the confusion between one route and all routes

questions.explanation: The account is good and the conclusion uses it for a question it cannot answer. A member can describe the telephone route in detail because they know it, and can report their own impression that most callers ring, and both of those are worth having; neither is a count of how the callers came. The claim the group wants to make, that almost nobody uses the counter, is a frequency claim, and frequency comes from a record of how the bookings arrived, which the office presumably has. The fourth option names the error precisely, since detail and coverage are different virtues and a perfectly detailed account of one route says nothing about the others. The second is an objection about the witness that does not touch the reasoning, and the third resolves it the wrong way by choosing testimony over counting.
questions.hint: Ask whether the conclusion is about one route or about how often each route is used.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Why the way of asking changes what the answer records
questions.learningObjective: explain why a method of elicitation is part of the evidence it produces
questions.stem: Explain why a way of asking is part of the evidence a group's record contains, and what a group should do about it.

answer.exemplar: Every record of what people said was produced by a particular encounter, and the encounter decided some of what could be said. A schedule that puts the difficult question last has let the easy questions set the frame, and whatever the person concludes by the time the hard one arrives has been shaped by the four before it. A question that names the finding the researcher suspects has supplied the answer and the agreement that follows is partly the wording. An interviewer who is himself the designer of the thing being discussed has made criticism expensive, and the resulting uniformity is a fact about the room. What follows is not that interviews are worthless, since they are often the only route to a practice nobody has written down, but that the group has to treat the instrument as part of the record rather than as a transparent window. In practice this means three things. First, publish the schedule with the report, so a reader can see the order and the phrasing, which is a disclosure almost nobody makes and which costs nothing. Second, vary the instrument for the claims that matter most: ask about a specific recent occasion rather than about a routine in general, since a specific occasion can be checked against other records and a general one cannot. Third, triangulate, so a claim resting on one interview is corroborated by a log, a form, or a person at another point in the chain, and a claim resting on all three is reported as the strong thing it is. A group that reports its instrument alongside its findings has done the harder and more useful thing, because the reader can then judge the finding rather than the reader's trust in the group.

questions.explanation: A strong response explains that the encounter produces part of the record, giving concrete mechanisms such as the order of the questions, the phrasing that supplies an answer, and the interviewer's own stake; that the conclusion is not that elicitation is worthless but that the instrument belongs in the report; and that the remedies are to publish the schedule, to ask about specific recent occasions rather than routines in general, and to corroborate interview claims against logs, forms, or people at other points in the chain. It should also note that a method is not a disqualification, so that the answer does not collapse into refusing to interview anyone.
questions.hint: Ask what the respondent would have said if the question had been put in a different order or a different tone.
