questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Why a figure with a caveat beats one without
questions.learningObjective: explain what a caveat on a figure does for the reader
questions.stem: Explain why a figure reported with its caveat is more useful to a reader than the same figure reported on its own.

answer.exemplar: A bare figure is a number with the reader expected to supply the parts that would let them use it, and readers supply them differently, which is why two people given the same number will argue about it in incompatible ways. Resolution ran at 78 per cent in each of three years: without the note, a reader concludes the service held steady; with the note, a reader concludes the service reported the same rate over a period in which the count was changed once, which is a different and more useful sentence. The caveat is doing three jobs. It names the population the figure is a rate of, so the reader can tell whether it is the population they had in mind. It names the conditions under which the rate was produced, so a reader who knows the conditions can discount the figure appropriately rather than accepting or rejecting it wholesale. And it records what the group did not do, which is the part a reader most needs and the part a report is most inclined to leave out, since a group knows its own omissions better than anyone. There is a real cost, which is that a caveated figure is less quotable and a bare one gets repeated, so the remedy is to keep the figure and the caveat in the same sentence so that a reader who carries the number away carries the condition with it. The test of a good caveat is that it changes what a reader would do, and if it would not, it is decoration and should be cut.

questions.explanation: A strong response explains that a bare figure leaves the reader to supply its population, its conditions, and the group's omissions, and that readers supply them inconsistently, so a number travels into arguments it cannot support. It should show the resolution-rate case concretely, in which the caveat turns a claim of steadiness into a claim about a series with a changed count. It should give the three jobs a caveat does, name the population, name the conditions, and record what was not done, and it should acknowledge the cost, that a caveated figure is less quotable, together with the test of whether a caveat would change what a reader would do.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would conclude from the bare number, and what they would conclude with the note attached.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Why an unobtainable document is a different kind of evidence
questions.learningObjective: explain how losing the ability to re-observe a document changes its evidential status
questions.stem: Explain why a document a group can no longer obtain is a different kind of evidence from one it can re-read, and what a group should do about it.

answer.exemplar: The weight of a document comes partly from what a reader can do with it, and a document nobody can obtain has lost part of that weight permanently rather than temporarily. A group that can re-read a page can check the date against the surrounding entries, see whether the signature is in the same hand throughout, notice the qualification two paragraphs down, and ask the archivist whether the volume was rearranged. A group holding a note of the same page can do none of that, and no amount of care will supply it. The status of the copy is therefore a matter of degree and should be described in words rather than assumed: a group can hold the original, a certified copy, a photocopy, a transcription, a quotation, or a note of one, and these are six different evidentiary positions, routinely reported as one. What a group should do follows from the description. Record which of the six the group holds and date it, so that a later reader knows what the group could and could not have checked. Quote sparingly and paraphrase the rest, so that the wording carried in the report is the group's own and is answerable for. Treat anything a reader might dispute as provisional and mark it, and separate the part of the claim that depends on the document from the part that does not, so that losing the document costs the argument one step rather than all of it. The temptation is to argue as though the copy were the original, which is not dishonesty so much as a failure to notice that two different objects are being called by one name.

questions.explanation: A strong response explains that a document's evidential weight includes what a reader can do with it, that a copy nobody can obtain has permanently lost the checks of date, hand, context, and completeness, and that the resulting status is a matter of degree to be named rather than assumed. It should distinguish the original, a certified copy, a photocopy, a transcription, a quotation, and a note of one as six different positions. It should give the practical steps: record which the group holds and when, quote sparingly, mark the provisional parts, and separate the claims that depend on the document from those that do not, so the argument loses one step rather than all of it.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader could check about a document they are holding, and then what they could not.

questions.topic: A minute that records an intention rather than an act
questions.learningObjective: state what a decision to publish does and does not establish about publication
questions.stem: A group holds a 1971 minute recording that a records schedule would be published. The schedule itself was destroyed in 1980. A member writes that the group published the schedule in 1971. What is the state of that claim?

options.text: The minute records a decision, and the group's own claim to have published rests on a document nobody can see
Settled, since a minute is a contemporary record of the group's own act and needs no support
options.misconception: mistakes a record of a decision for a record of the thing the decision was about

options.text: Refuted, since a document that no longer exists cannot be produced in answer to the claim
options.misconception: turns the group's inability to produce the document into a fact against the claim

options.text: A matter of preference, since nobody can now be expected to settle a question about 1971
options.misconception: declines a question the minute and its own limits are enough to state in one sentence

questions.explanation: A minute is a record of what a group decided, and publication is a separate act that the minute cannot report. The claim that the schedule appeared in 1971 needs something the group does not have, and the honest report has two sentences: the group resolved in 1971 to publish a records schedule, and no copy of the schedule survives, so the group cannot show that it was published. That is a weaker claim and a usable one. The second option is the error every minute-based history repeats, since the record of a decision is treated as the record of the world the decision was about. The third goes the other way and makes an archival loss into a refutation, which is not what a missing document shows. The fourth is a surrender: the group knows exactly what it holds, and one sentence of candour settles the question without anyone having to prefer anything.
questions.hint: Ask what a minute is a record of, and what act would have to be recorded separately.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Checking a claim against the record that produced it
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of testing a claim against a record so each depends on the one before
questions.stem: A group has a claim and a record. Put the steps in the order that lets each depend on the one before it.

options.text: State the claim as something the record could show or hide, since a vague claim cannot be checked
List what the record actually contains on that point, since this is the side of the test nobody often skips
Look for anything in the record that bears against the claim, since support alone settles nothing
Report the claim with what the record did and did not settle, since both belong in the sentence

questions.explanation: The order runs from the claim to the sentence that will carry it. The claim first, stated as something the record could show or hide, because a claim phrased as a mood cannot be checked by anything and a group that skips this step will spend the discussion comparing the record with its own paraphrase. What the record contains second, which is the step most often skipped and the one that decides whether the test is worth running at all, since a record that shows nothing relevant settles nothing. The search for what bears against the claim third, and it is third because a group that has only looked for support has not tested anything, only confirmed. The report last, in one sentence carrying the claim and its limits together, because a reader given only the first will over-read it. Any other order leaves a step with nothing to work on: the reporting before the search, or the search before the claim has been made checkable.
questions.hint: Ask which step, done first, leaves the three after it with nothing to apply to the record.

questions.topic: A count that rose while the room was open for fewer days
questions.learningObjective: compute what an opening-hours change does to a before-and-after count
questions.stem: A group's report says attendance at the reading room rose by half after new opening hours. Its own log shows 40 sign-ins in the eleven days before the change, with the room shut for two of them, and 61 in the eleven days after, with the room open throughout. Four readings follow. Which is the strongest supported judgement?

options.text: Attendance rose by half, since 61 is about half as many again as 40 and the counts are the counts
options.misconception: accepts the raw count, where the two periods contained a different number of open days

options.text: The report is wrong, since a rise in a count is not a rise in anything the change brought about
options.misconception: over-corrects, denying a genuine increase in order to avoid the adjustment the report needed

options.text: The report should be withdrawn, since a pair of eleven-day periods cannot support any claim at all
options.misconception: discards a comparison that is merely incomplete, and removes the two figures a reader needs

options.text: The count rose from 40 to 61 while the room was shut for fewer days, so the rise per open day is smaller

questions.explanation: The count rose from 40 to 61, which is a rise of about 52 per cent, and the two periods did not contain the same opportunity: the room was shut for two of the earlier eleven days and open for all eleven of the later ones. Per open day that is about 4.4 sign-ins before and about 5.5 after, a rise of roughly a quarter rather than a half. Both figures point the same way, so the direction is not in question; the report's figure overstates the size because it compares a count from nine open days with a count from eleven. The honest sentence gives the counts and the open days together. The second option is the over-correction, and the third throws away a comparison that two small corrections would make sound, which is the opposite of what a careful group should do.
questions.hint: Divide each count by the number of days the room was actually open in that period.
